newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels advance, refugees die in hundreds.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels advance, refugees die in hundreds.

text.p: More rebel progress was reported in Zaire's mineral-rich Shaba province on Friday as harrowing proof emerged that Hutu refugees are dying in their hundreds from disease and hunger.

Despite agreeing to negotiate in the next days with President Mobutu Sese Seko's shaky government, Laurent Kabila's rebels captured the town of Kasenga on Friday, expatriate sources in the Shaba capital Lubumbashi said.
A Defence Ministry official in Kinshasa denied the report. The rebels control a quarter of the vast country, five months after launching the revolt to topple the ailing Mobutu, 66.

In and around Ubilo, a village 82 km (50 miles) south of rebel-held Kisangani in northeastern Zaire, aid workers and journalists saw the appalling plight of about 75,000 of the Rwandan Hutu refugees trapped in the war zone.
At least 500 have been buried since March 16 at Ubilo, according to Lubinga Nganda, head of a Zairean Red Cross team.
Emaciated refugees, some almost skeletal, were attempting to walk towards aid at Kisangani but those too weak to start the trek lay dead and dying within the abandoned Ubilo camp.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it found 20 unburied bodies at Ubilo while at a temporary transit camp nearby journalists watched a baby die in its mother's arms.

The refugees huddling along a railway line are dying of malaria, dysentery, fatigue and malnutrition, a Zairean Red Cross nurse said. Aid workers brought the first 120 tonnes of food and medicine by train on Thursday and Friday.
"There has been a selection. The fittest make it but the unfit die," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, a UNHCR emergency officer, surveying the scene at Ubilo.
Local people said the Zairean rebels attacked and killed at least 100 armed refugees in two incidents last week.

Former Rwandan soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen, responsible for the genocide of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994, are among up to 370,000 refugees still roaming around eastern Zaire.
Care, protection and repatriation of the refugees is part of a five-point U.N. peace plan to end the civil war in Zaire.
The two sides agreed at an African summit in Togo this week to open negotiations, probably in South Africa.
The rebels have rejected a prior ceasefire and say the issue is not whether Mobutu transfers power but how and when his 32-year-old regime comes to an end.
"I think rebel strategy centres around talking while fighting and fighting while talking," a regional military source told Reuters in Nairobi.
A senior rebel official said the talks would start next Monday or Tuesday and a government source in South Africa confirmed a meeting was on the cards.
But in Kinshasa, Mobutu's spokesman rejected the rebel agenda and denied a firm date for talks had yet been agreed.
Professor Kabuya Lumuna said the talks might lead to a transitional government before elections at which Mobutu has previously said he will be a candidate.
"We are at a stage of proposals, and not diktats," he told Reuters.
"President Mobutu remains the head of state. The people of Zaire are free to contest the person of Mr Mobutu in elections but not the institution of head of state," Kabuya said.
The rebels, piling on the pressure before any talks, say their next targets are Lubumbashi, the Shaba capital, and Zaire's diamond centre, Mbuji-Mayi.

Shaba sits on some of the world's biggest deposits of copper, cobalt and precious metals. Kabila's officials are already meeting foreign mining companies about future concessions, industry sources say.
Despite the Defence Ministry denial, the foreign sources in Lubumbashi insisted the alliance's disciplined fighters captured Kasenga, 220 km (135 miles) to the north, on Friday.
"It is definitely rebel troops who are in control of Kasenga," one source with contacts in Kasenga told Reuters.
He and other sources, who declined to be identified, said it was a lightning takeover and by midday the town of about 17,000 people on the Luapula river bordering Zambia was quiet.
Zaire's demoralised army, the FAZ, has failed to hold any ground threatened by the rebels during the war. They usually go on violent looting sprees before retreating.
